column5: cloud, rain, grass made to grow
column6: The psalm supplies the causal sequence left unspoken in 87:4: God covers the sky with clouds, prepares rain for earth, and makes grass grow. It places the brought-forth pasture between the cloud's appearance and its nourishment.

column5: grass for cattle and food from earth
column6: God causes grass to grow for cattle and vegetation to yield human food. This makes explicit the commentary's claim that merʿā is grass seen as sustenance for animals and, through them, people.

column5: God makes grass sprout in desolation
column6: In God's speech to Job, rain satisfies the waste land and causes tender grass to sprout. It is a close divine-agent counterpart to bringing pasture out of apparently barren ground.

column5: grass for livestock, then human satiety
column6: God promises grass in the fields for Israel's livestock before saying that Israel will eat and be satisfied. The animal-before-human order directly illuminates the commentary's food chain around pasture.

column5: rain for seed and broad pasture
column6: God gives rain to seed sown in the ground, rich bread from its produce, and broad pasture for livestock. It joins the commentary's rain, growth, food, and grazing scenes in one verse.

column5: rain waters earth, sprouting, seed and bread
column6: Rain and snow water the earth so that it brings forth and sprouts, supplying seed to the sower and bread to the eater. This gives the full hidden-to-edible growth sequence developed from 87:4.

column5: God causes growth out of ground
column6: The LORD God causes trees to sprout out of the ground. Its divine causation and movement from earth into visible life closely match the commentary's concrete sense of إخراج.

column5: morning sprouting and evening withering
column6: Human life is compared to grass that sprouts in the morning and fades and withers in the evening. It gives a tightly ordered life-and-loss counterpart to 87:4–5's green pasture becoming dark debris.

column5: grass withers under the LORD's breath
column6: Grass withers and flower fades when the breath of the LORD blows on it. The verse sharpens the commentary's insistence that the pasture's end, like its emergence, remains under divine action.

column5: withering grass and enduring divine word
column6: After grass withers and flowers fade, God's word stands forever. This is a particularly close counterpart to the commentary's contrast between perishable vegetation and the recited word that is not forgotten.

column5: chaff driven by wind
column6: The wicked are likened to chaff driven away by wind. It gives a Hebrew-scriptural use of dry vegetal waste that helps read 87:5's transformed pasture as an image of passing and loss.

column5: God opens graves and brings people up
column6: God promises to open Israel's graves and bring the people up from them. It is a direct second-emergence counterpart to the commentary's move from vegetation coming out of earth to the dead being brought out.

column5: dead in dust awaken
column6: The dead live, those dwelling in dust awake, and the earth gives birth to the dead. The earth-to-life movement directly accompanies the commentary's claim that pasture makes resurrection imaginable.

column5: awakening from dust to two outcomes
column6: Those sleeping in the dust awaken, some to everlasting life and some to shame. It closely parallels the commentary's second emergence and its insistence that the final state divides into contrasting outcomes.

column5: Midianite daughters at the well with their flock
column6: Exodus places Moses at a Midian well where the priest's daughters arrive to water their father's flock. It is the same narrative setting behind the commentary's two women, livestock, and Moses at Midian.

column5: Moses helps and waters the flock
column6: Moses intervenes for the women and waters their flock. This is the specific action that stands beside the commentary's account of Musa watering the women's animals before his pastoral years.

column5: Moses shepherding Jethro's flock at Horeb
column6: Moses is tending Jethro's flock when he leads it to Horeb. It directly matches the commentary's portrait of Musa as a shepherd before the fire and prophetic call.

column5: Hebrew מִרְעֶה and רעה, pasture and shepherding
column6: Hebrew mirʿeh, “pasture,” and the verb rʿh, “to shepherd/feed,” are cognate with the commentary's merʿā and rāʿā family. Ezekiel's God feeds the flock in good pasture, making explicit the pastoral semantic field that 87:4 evokes without naming God a shepherd.

column5: earth gives up those sleeping in it
column6: The apocalypse says that the earth will give up those who sleep in it and the dust those who rest in silence. It supplies a Jewish articulation of the commentary's earth-to-resurrection inference.

column5: earth restores the dead it received
column6: 2 Baruch imagines the earth returning the dead it has received and preserved. Its soil as temporary keeper of bodies closely corresponds to the commentary's “another bringing out” from ground.

column5: rain from heaven, fruitful seasons, food
column6: Paul's speech describes God giving rains from heaven and fruitful seasons, filling people with food and gladness. It is a direct Christian-scriptural analogue for 87:4's providential pasture as nourishment.

column5: grass today and oven tomorrow
column6: Jesus calls the grass of the field present today and thrown into an oven tomorrow, while stressing God's care for it. This matches the commentary's abrupt movement from green pasture to a fire-adjacent perishable end.

column5: seed secretly sprouts and grows
column6: In the seed parable, the sower sleeps and rises while the seed sprouts and grows in a way he does not know. It closely reflects the commentary's hidden seed and root becoming visible vegetation beyond human control.

column5: earth yields blade, ear, full grain
column6: The earth produces first a blade, then an ear, then full grain. Its staged growth gives a New Testament counterpart to the commentary's water-to-plant-to-green-to-grain sequence.

column5: rain-drinking land produces useful crop
column6: Land drinks rain and produces a useful crop, receiving blessing from God. The verse aligns rain, productive soil, and divine blessing with the commentary's pasture as a granted provision.

column5: land yielding thorns ends in burning
column6: The immediately contrasted land yields thorns and thistles and ends in burning. It gives a specific Christian counterpart to the commentary's patchy fertile and barren ground, and to vegetation's ominous end.

column5: planting, watering, God giving growth
column6: Paul distinguishes his planting and Apollos's watering from God giving the growth. It directly supports the commentary's pedagogical extension: human teaching may cultivate, but emergence and maturation belong to God.

column5: God alone gives growth
column6: Neither planter nor waterer is decisive, but God who makes things grow. This is an unusually exact counterpart to the page's focus on who, rather than what mechanism, brings pasture forth.

column5: seed dies before coming to life
column6: Paul answers the resurrection question by saying a sown thing does not come to life unless it dies. It gives the commentary's pasture-to-resurrection reasoning a direct agricultural form.

column5: bare grain is sown before its future body
column6: The passage identifies the sown object as bare grain rather than the body it will become. It makes concrete the commentary's contrast between hidden seed, visible plant, and a later embodied emergence.

column5: God gives the seed its body
column6: God gives the seed a body as he wills. This attributes the transition from grain to formed life to divine choice, like 87:4's attribution of pasture's coming forth.

column5: all in tombs hear and come out
column6: Jesus says all who are in the tombs will hear his voice and come out. It is a direct verbal and conceptual counterpart to the commentary's second خروج from the earth.

column5: coming out to life or judgment
column6: Those who come out do so to resurrection of life or resurrection of judgment. This supplies the two final destinations which the commentary sets after vegetation's single temporary course.

column5: all flesh as grass that withers
column6: The epistle quotes the grass-and-flower image for mortal flesh. It is a close Christian reuse of the same vegetal transience that the commentary reads from 87:4 into 87:5.

column5: enduring word after grass's fading
column6: The Lord's word remains forever after the preceding grass image. Like the commentary's comparison of fading pasture with unforgotten recitation, it contrasts transient vegetation with enduring proclamation.

column5: buried seed rises as proof of resurrection
column6: 1 Clement uses a seed sown dry and naked in earth, then rising into life, as an argument for resurrection. It is a close early Christian interpretation of the natural cycle that the commentary presents as evidence for a second emergence.

column5: livestock fed before a person eats
column6: The Talmud reads Deuteronomy 11:15's order as forbidding a person to eat before feeding an animal. That interpretation develops precisely the commentary's observation that pasture first sustains the herd.

column5: Moses's care for a lamb proves him fit to lead Israel
column6: The midrash makes Moses's compassionate shepherding the test that qualifies him to shepherd Israel. It directly develops the commentary's passage from Musa's flock, staff, and care to the shepherd-leader sense of the root.

column5: God commands earth to sprout seed-bearing vegetation
column6: God commands the earth to sprout vegetation, seed-bearing plants, and fruit trees according to kinds. It contributes the created order and measured differentiation that surround 87:4 in the commentary.

column5: God shepherded Jacob all his life
column6: Jacob calls God the one who shepherded him throughout his life. It offers a personal divine-shepherd use of the Hebrew cognate field beside the commentary's cautious pastoral associations of merʿā.

column5: shepherding as skilled political guidance
column6: David shepherds Israel with integrity and guides them with skillful hands. It realizes the commentary's extension from grazing and guarding a flock to leadership that sees a people toward its end.

column5: God reveals hidden things and knows darkness
column6: God reveals deep and hidden things and knows what is in darkness. This gives a biblical counterpart to the commentary's linkage of hidden seed, what is brought out, and God's knowledge of concealed things.

column5: bringing prisoners out of darkness
column6: The servant's commission includes bringing prisoners out of a dungeon and those sitting in darkness into light. It provides a specific biblical analogue to the commentary's secondary movement from hidden darkness to an instructed, illuminated human life.

column5: teaching as rain and dew on grass
column6: Moses compares his teaching to rain and dew falling on tender grass and vegetation. It joins the page's rain-grown pasture to its later account of instruction that brings people beyond ignorance.

column5: harvest's edge left for poor and resident alien
column6: The harvest owner must leave the field's edge and gleanings for the poor and alien. It is a concrete Torah counterpart to the commentary's claim that what the ground yields carries a due share for others.

column5: firstfruits brought before God in worship
column6: Israel brings the first of the ground's fruit before the LORD and bows in worship. It pairs agricultural yield with praise, echoing the commentary's ordering of divine provision and sanctifying the Lord's name.

column5: water and food without money or price
column6: The thirsty are invited to water, wine, and milk without money or price. Its gratuitous food image gives a close biblical analogue to the commentary's provision and admonition offered without demanded payment.

column5: God needs no food from creatures
column6: God says that if hungry he would not tell humans, since the world and its fullness are his. It clarifies the commentary's claim that the giver of pasture does not need a return payment from those who live on it.

column5: being sent out of the garden to the ground
column6: The LORD sends the human out of Eden to work the ground from which he was taken. It gives a specific biblical instance of the commentary's secondary sense of “bringing out” as removal from an inhabited place rather than plant emergence.

column5: brought out in order to be brought in
column6: God brings Israel out from Egypt in order to bring them into the promised land. The out/in pair closely accompanies the commentary's semantic contrast between departure from a place and entry into one.

column5: life made in secret in earth-like depths
column6: The psalmist's frame is not hidden when made in secret and woven in the depths of the earth. It extends the commentary's unseen earth imagery from seed to the hidden beginning of human life.

column5: God renews the face of the ground
column6: When God sends his spirit, creatures are created and the face of the ground is renewed. It is a natural-renewal analogue for the commentary's annual revivification of dead land.

column5: earth's sprouts image righteousness and praise
column6: As earth brings forth sprouts and a garden makes seed sprout, God causes righteousness and praise to sprout. This is a precise biblical bridge between vegetation emerging from soil and the commentary's cultivation of human understanding.

column5: peah and firstfruits among required agricultural gifts
column6: The Mishnah lists the field-corner gift and firstfruits among practices without a fixed measure. It gives Jewish legal shape to the commentary's harvest-as-yield that is not merely possessed but bears a claim for others.

column5: rain compared with resurrection
column6: The Talmud compares the day of rain with the resurrection of the dead. That explicit rabbinic pairing makes visible the inferential bridge from rain-fed revival of land to resurrection that the commentary draws.

column5: good soil receives the word and bears fruit
column6: Jesus interprets the good soil as hearers who receive the word and bear fruit. It changes the commentary's physically uneven soil into a teaching image, making the interpretive bridge explicit rather than assuming it.

column5: commission to turn people from darkness to light
column6: Paul's commission opens eyes and turns people from darkness to light. It closely parallels the commentary's secondary use of bringing out as education and deliverance from darkness.

column5: hidden things of darkness brought to light
column6: At judgment the Lord brings to light what is hidden in darkness and discloses hearts' purposes. It gives a Christian counterpart to the commentary's hidden seed and divine disclosure of what lies concealed.

column5: freely received, freely give
column6: Jesus tells the disciples to give freely because they received freely. It specifically parallels the commentary's extension from freely given pasture to an admonitory ministry that asks no fee.

column5: gospel offered without charge
column6: Paul describes making the gospel free of charge rather than using his right to support. This is the concrete apostolic counterpart to the commentary's unpaid teaching and uncharged provision.

column5: shepherding God's flock through oversight
column6: Elders are told to shepherd God's flock while exercising oversight. It closely matches the commentary's semantic account in which grazing, guarding, and watchful responsibility belong together.

column5: good shepherd gives life for sheep
column6: Jesus identifies himself as the good shepherd who lays down his life for the sheep. It offers the specifically Christian development of the shepherd image lying at the edge of the commentary's merʿā-root reflection.

column5: light from darkness gives knowledge
column6: The Creator who commanded light from darkness shines in hearts to give knowledge. It joins creation, illumination, and learning in the manner of the commentary's move from soil-darkness to instruction.

column5: world passes but God's doer remains
column6: The world and its desire pass away, but the one who does God's will remains forever. It supplies a Christian ethical form of the commentary's contrast between transient pasture and what is more enduring.

column5: sun withers grass and rich person's flower falls
column6: The sun's heat withers grass and makes its flower fall while the rich person fades in pursuits. It gives another focused New Testament use of vegetal decline for the passing human condition.

column5: grain dies and bears much fruit
column6: A grain of wheat falls into earth and dies in order to bear much fruit. It forms a Christological transformation of the seed-death-and-new-life pattern the commentary applies to pasture and later emergence.

column5: the hidden will become manifest
column6: Nothing hidden remains without becoming manifest and coming to light. It parallels the commentary's secondary association of bringing forth with making the concealed visible.

column5: seen things temporary, unseen eternal
column6: The visible is temporary while the unseen is eternal. It gives a concise Christian analogue for the commentary's contrast of what emerges and perishes in this world with the lasting final reality.

column5: God feeds birds without their sowing or harvesting
column6: The heavenly Father feeds birds that neither sow nor reap nor store. It complements the commentary's pasture-as-provision theme by making divine feeding independent of the creatures' own agricultural control.
